plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LY10 creating spoken persuasive texts; VC2E5LE04 language that evokes emotion; VC2E5LA07 cohesion with signposts
plan.shape: model, guide, apply: the teacher drafts arguments 2 and 3 with a true small story, students zoom big claims into small stories, then draft the middle of their own speech
plan.criticalFeature: one true small story beats ten big claims: a who, a where, a what happened
decisionPoints: the Big claim or small story? round
the choice check: the moment that moves us
the exit board: a small story for a new claim
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Say it. Today: Sell it, with a story they can see.
plan.catchUp: Students without an S3 opening draft argument 3 with a story only.

studentTools: S2 proof and S3 opening (in the speech folder)
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: A small story: who, where, what happened, link back
Signposts: First... On top of that... But most importantly...

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: spot small stories, zoom in on big claims, sort the signposts, then draft the middle of your speech.
resources.title: The Heart of the Speech
resources.subtitle: Zoom in. Make them feel it.

example.prompt: Last week, a magpie got stuck in a chip packet.
steps: Is there a where or when?
example.answer: A small story: a who, a when and a happening.

items.prompt: Plastic is a huge problem everywhere.
On Tuesday, Zara's lunch bag blew into the creek.
Lots of kids get hurt crossing roads.

example.answer: Sam waited for pickup in the sun. Forty minutes. Burnt shoulders.

items.prompt: Turn each big claim into a small story.
rows: Crossing the road here is dangerous.
answers: At the beach, my brother found a gull tangled in fishing line.
Last night I watched one more video. Then it was 11 pm.
Crossing the road here is dangerous.
Yesterday a car missed my friend by a metre at the gate.

example.answer: First, then On top of that, then But most importantly.

items.prompt: Sort the signposts: FIRST, MIDDLE or LAST.
items.hint: Which ones say the best is coming?

example.answer: On top of that, our yard hit 41 degrees. But most importantly... Sam's burnt shoulders.

items.prompt: Write argument 2 with a signpost and its proof.
items.answer: A signpost, argument 2 and its proof, in short sentences.

items.prompt: Write argument 3, your strongest, with a small true story.
items.answer: But most importantly... argument 3 with a who, where and what happened.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: add senses to small stories, then retell your story to change the feeling.
resources.title: Paint the Picture
resources.subtitle: Help them see it, hear it, feel it.

example.prompt: Sam waited for pickup in the sun.
example.answer: Sam waited by the gate. No shade. The bench burnt through his shorts.

items.prompt: Add a sense to each small story.
rows: A gull was tangled in fishing line.
The yard was hot at lunch.
A car nearly hit my friend.
answers: A gull was tangled in fishing line.
It flapped and squawked, the line cutting its leg.
The yard was hot at lunch.
The slide burnt my legs. The air shimmered.
A car nearly hit my friend.
Brakes screeched. My heart thumped. One metre.

example.answer: Hopeful: we cut the line, and it flew away. That's what action does.

items.prompt: Retell your own small story twice: once to make us worried, once to make us hopeful.
items.answer: Two versions of the student's story with clearly different feelings.

items.prompt: One day, ___. It was ___. That's why ___.
items.answer: A small true story linked to the claim.
items.hint: Think of something that really happened.

slides.notes: Open S4. One line: today we write the part of the speech they will remember.
Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it. Students need their S2 proof and S3 opening.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to use a small true story to make an audience feel our argument.
successCriteria: I can tell a big claim from a small story.
I can write my middle arguments with signposts and a small story.
I can add senses so the audience can picture it.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Big claims tell. Small stories make people feel.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: The first one is where we all start.
The second one is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 is reachable for all; SC2 is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 is the stretch.

slides.title: Which one do you feel?
lines: 1: Millions of animals are harmed by plastic.
2: Last week a magpie got its head stuck in a chip packet. It couldn't eat.

beats: SAY: Two lines. Same message.
ASK: Which one do you feel more? 1 or 2?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: 2
ASK: Why does the smaller one hit harder?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: I can see it; it's one bird; it's real
SAY: Millions is too big to picture. One magpie, you can see.
trap: thinking bigger numbers always persuade more.
Fix: ask which one could you picture?
notes.prep: Low-entry launch. Severn and Malala both used small true moments. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: A short true story told to make a point.
slides.example: Sam's burnt shoulders are my anecdote.

notes.answer: a short true story told to make a point
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Anecdote. Say it with me. Anecdote.
SAY: A short true story told to make a point.
SAY: Sam's burnt shoulders are my anecdote.
ASK: What makes an anecdote different from a big claim?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: a who, a where, something that happened
trap: Fix: say true and small beats invented and huge.

slides.title: Writing the heart of my speech

rows: On top of that, shade keeps us cool. In February our yard hit 41 degrees.
But most importantly, shade protects our skin. Shade cuts UV by up to 75%.
Last summer, Sam waited for pickup in the sun. Forty minutes. Burnt shoulders.
One tree would have stopped that.

notes.answer: signpost, argument, proof, then a small story that links back
beats: POINT to the signposts.
SAY: On top of that. But most importantly. The ear hears the best is coming.
POINT to Anecdote.
SAY: I zoom in. One kid. One place. What happened.
Short sentences, so they can see it.
POINT to Link back.
SAY: The story must point back to my claim, or it's just a story.
ASK: What three things does my anecdote have?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: who, where, what happened
trap: a story that never links back to the claim.
Fix: ask so what? Student adds the link-back line.
notes.stretch: Add a sense: what Sam felt or heard.
notes.help: Use the frame: One day... It was... That's why...
notes.prep: Model with a real or realistic small moment from your own school. Critical feature: one small true story.

slides.title: Big claim or small story?
slides.pivot: ask is there a who, a where and a happening?
slides.followUp: cold call one student: which detail tells you?

items.text: At swimming, Noah found a straw in the pool filter.
Many families struggle to afford food.
My grandpa planted a tree the year I was born.
Last Friday our class bin overflowed by lunch.

say: One finger: big claim. Two: small story.
trap: calling any sad sentence a story.
Fix: ask who is it about? When did it happen?
notes.stretch: Zoom one big claim into a story.
notes.help: Look for a name and a day.

options.text: Lots of people get sunburnt, which is bad.
options.misconception: a big claim; nothing to picture

options.text: Sam waited in the sun for forty minutes. His shoulders blistered.
It is very, very, very sad and terrible.
options.misconception: tells us to feel; shows nothing

notes.answer: B - a who, a where and what happened
beats: SAY: Three tries at the emotional moment.
ASK: Which moment moves us most?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: what can you picture in B?
Less -> read each, ask what can you see? re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. We can see Sam. We don't need to be told it's sad.
trap: pointing to C because it has the most feeling words.
Fix: ask what can you see in C? Nothing.
notes.prep: Decision point before drafting. Under 80% means one more zoom-in done together.

slides.title: Zoom in
slides.pivot: write a name, then a place, then one thing that happened
slides.followUp: cold call one board: read it like a speaker

items.answer: e.g. Mia ate lunch alone for a week. Nobody asked why.
items.expect: a who, a where, a happening

items.text: Big claim: our oceans are full of rubbish.
items.answer: e.g. At Torquay, I picked up 40 bottle caps in ten minutes.
items.expect: a who, a where, a happening

items.text: Big claim: kids need more sleep.
items.answer: e.g. On Monday, Leo fell asleep in maths. Head on the desk.
items.expect: a who, a where, a happening

say: Turn the big claim into a small story. Two short sentences.
trap: repeating the big claim with a name added.
Fix: ask what happened? Student adds one action.
notes.help: Use: One day, ___ was at ___ and ___.

slides.title: Draft the middle
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet. Finish by drafting arguments 2 and 3 of your speech, with signposts and a small true story.
slides.frame: On top of that, ___. But most importantly, ___. One day, ___.

notes.answer: arguments 2 and 3 with signposts, proof and a small true story
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Arguments 2 and 3, with signposts and your small true story.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Ask: who is in your story? What happened? Does it link back?
ASK: Read your story to your partner. What could they picture?
40 sec each. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: a who, a where, a happening
trap: a story with no link back to the argument.
Fix: student adds That's why... at the end.
notes.stretch: Extension: add the senses, then change the feeling.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: picture-clue choices, a zoom-in done, a frame.
notes.prep: Independent drafting; S5 writes the finish and cue cards. SC2.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in the student's drafted arguments 2 and 3 with an anecdote

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Big claim: junk food ads target kids.
Write a small story that makes an audience feel it: who, where, what happened.

notes.answer: e.g. On Saturday, my sister begged for nuggets after one TV ad.
beats: SAY: A new big claim. Zoom it in.
ASK: Write a small story: who, where, what happened.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: a name, a place, a happening
RECORD who writes another big claim. Conference list for S5.
trap: another big claim instead of a story.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new claim. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Who in your speech will your audience picture?

notes.answer: open - a name from their story
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that your story links back to your argument?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Who in your speech will your audience picture?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: a name from their story
notes.prep: Drafts go in the speech folder for S5. SC2.
